paragraphs: Incremental semantic segmentation asks a model to keep learning new categories of pixels without losing its ability to recognize earlier categories. This is especially difficult when each training stage supplies labels only for the new categories. Previously learned objects can still appear in images, but their pixels no longer provide explicit supervision for their old labels.

ALIFE combines a change to the learning objective with a more compact form of memory. The authors analyze probability calibration techniques used to extract semantic information from unlabeled pixels, then introduce an adaptive regularizer on the model’s prediction scores. It is designed to support learning new categories while preserving earlier knowledge.

The memory component stores features instead of complete images, reducing storage requirements. Because the feature extractor changes during learning, ALIFE updates stored features using a separate rotation matrix for each category. Experiments on standard benchmarks show a better balance between accuracy and efficiency, supporting the combination of adaptive regularization and updated feature replay.
neurips-2022-alife-adaptive-logit-regula.tldr: ALIFE combines adaptive regularization with updated feature memories to improve the accuracy–efficiency tradeoff in incremental semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised few-shot learning asks a classifier to adapt to a new task using very few labeled examples and a fixed collection of unlabeled examples. The labeled examples form the support set: the small amount of direct evidence available about the task’s categories. The challenge is to make the unlabeled examples useful despite this shortage of supervision.

The paper proposes learning indirectly through negative pseudo-labels. These labels identify categories that an unlabeled example should not belong to, rather than directly assigning it a positive category. The method predicts accurate negative pseudo-labels and uses them to augment the information available from the support set.

This approach matters because supervision can include exclusions as well as positive identifications. The authors report that their method requires only a few lines of code and standard operations, yet outperforms state-of-the-art methods on four benchmark datasets. Those results establish that a simple use of negative information can be effective in the evaluated few-shot tasks.
neurips-2022-an-embarrassingly-simple-ap.tldr: A simple method uses negative pseudo-labels to make unlabeled examples useful for few-shot classification and outperforms existing methods on four benchmarks.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can struggle against convolutional networks when trained from scratch on small datasets. The paper identifies two relevant weaknesses in their built-in learning preferences: insufficient attention to neighboring image regions and insufficient diversity in channel representations. With little training data, the model may struggle to discover these useful patterns on its own.

Dynamic Hybrid Vision Transformer addresses spatial relationships by adding convolution to patch embedding and the multilayer perceptron module. These components make local neighborhoods part of feature extraction. For channel representations, the model adds dynamic feature aggregation and a head token mechanism, helping recalibrate channels and exchange information between channel groups.

The authors report closing the performance gap in their evaluations and obtaining state-of-the-art results with relatively lightweight models. Reported results include 85.68% on CIFAR-100 with 22.8 million parameters and 82.3% on ImageNet-1K with 24 million parameters. The findings support building local spatial structure and channel interaction directly into the architecture when learning them from limited data is difficult.
neurips-2022-bridging-the-gap-between-vi.tldr: DHVT adds local spatial processing and channel interaction to Vision Transformers, closing the reported performance gap with convolutional networks.

paragraphs: Referring image segmentation turns a natural-language description into a mask containing the pixels of the described object. Matching a sentence directly to individual pixels can overlook the fact that pixels belonging to one object should form a coherent whole. The paper links this weakness to incomplete masks and mistakes in locating the target.

CoupAlign combines alignment at two levels. First, its word-pixel module mixes language and visual features within intermediate encoder layers. The resulting features produce candidate object masks. A sentence-mask module then weights those candidates using the whole sentence and projects the result back to pixels to assemble the target mask.

An additional training loss contrasts foreground and background pixels to strengthen both alignment modules. Experiments report consistent improvements on datasets including RefCOCO and G-Ref, with about a 2% increase in overall intersection-over-union on RefCOCO validation and testing sets. The method also shows particular strength in selecting the intended object when several objects share the same class.
neurips-2022-coupalign-coupling-word-pix.tldr: CoupAlign connects word-level pixel matching with sentence-level object-mask matching to improve language-guided image segmentation.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to infer high-dimensional data using two sources of guidance: a prior describing plausible data and an additional constraint describing what a particular task requires. Its prior is an independently trained denoising diffusion model. The extra constraint depends on supplementary information and must have a differentiable form.

The proposed procedure performs approximate inference by repeatedly differentiating through the fixed denoising network. Each step incorporates a different amount of noise. This allows the search to evaluate candidate data through multiple noisy versions while retaining the same trained model as a reusable component.

The separation between the learned prior and the task constraint makes diffusion models potentially useful across new tasks and domains, including conditional generation and image segmentation. The constraint can vary without changing the independently trained prior. The authors also suggest that evaluating many noisy versions of a candidate may inspire algorithms for combinatorial optimization; this is presented as a possible direction, rather than an established general solution.
neurips-2022-diffusion-models-as-plug-an.tldr: A fixed diffusion model can serve as a reusable prior for approximate inference guided by differentiable task constraints.

paragraphs: Reducing a Vision Transformer’s operation count does not necessarily produce a matching increase in execution speed. This paper therefore makes measured speed on the target platform a design principle. It introduces LITv2, whose central mechanism, HiLo attention, separates processing for fine local details and broad image structure.

HiLo divides attention heads into two groups. One group operates within local windows to capture high-frequency detail. The other connects every query position to average-pooled keys and values from the windows, providing global attention through a coarser representation. This division gives local and global information different computational treatments within the attention layer.

The authors compare operation counts, speed, and memory use on both GPUs and CPUs. They report CPU speedups of 1.4 times over spatial reduction attention and 1.6 times over local window attention. LITv2 also performs favorably across model sizes and supports classification, detection, and segmentation. The results connect architectural efficiency to measured execution behavior, alongside its usefulness for vision tasks.
neurips-2022-fast-vision-transformers-wi.tldr: HiLo attention separates local detail from pooled global structure to give LITv2 faster measured execution and strong vision performance.

paragraphs: Quantization represents network values with fewer bits to make inference more efficient. This paper examines the additional flexibility of eight-bit floating point compared with eight-bit integers. Floating point can allocate bits between the mantissa and exponent, changing how numerical precision is distributed across values of different sizes.

The authors analyze settings in which particular FP8 choices perform better, then examine how those findings apply to real networks. They also provide an efficient FP8 simulation implementation and an algorithm that learns both scaling parameters and the number of exponent bits. This makes the numerical representation itself part of the optimization.

For post-training quantization across a wide range of networks, the authors find better accuracy with FP8 than INT8. The severity of unusually large values helps determine how many exponent bits are useful. In their quantization-aware training experiments, the difference between formats disappears as training reduces the influence of these outliers. The advantage therefore depends on how quantization interacts with the network’s value distribution and training.
neurips-2022-fp8-quantization-the-power-.tldr: FP8 improves post-training quantization accuracy across many evaluated networks, with its benefit tied to outliers and exponent allocation.

paragraphs: In the Neural Tangent Kernel regime, a network remains tied to its first-order approximation around initialization. This gives useful theory but does not capture feature learning. The abstract describes complementary strengths: the NTK handles dense polynomials well, while the second-order QuadNTK approach can efficiently learn sparse polynomials but loses the same ability on general dense ones.

The paper studies how a wide two-layer network can combine these strengths. A spectral analysis identifies directions in parameter space along which the network can move without harming generalization. Using these directions, the network can fit targets containing both a dense low-degree component and a sparse high-degree component.

The authors construct a regularizer that encourages movement along the identified directions. They prove that gradient descent on this regularized objective converges to a global minimizer with low test error in the studied setting. The resulting guarantee improves sample complexity over either NTK or QuadNTK alone, showing how controlled departures from lazy training can support both convergence and generalization.
neurips-2022-identifying-good-directions.tldr: A direction-selecting regularizer lets a wide two-layer network combine NTK and second-order learning with improved provable sample complexity.

paragraphs: Predicting which items users find relevant becomes difficult when a platform continually receives new content. A model trained on historical interactions faces a changing distribution of items and responses. The paper addresses this instability in settings such as recommendation systems, media services, and online marketplaces.

Its central idea is to account for how users believe their environment works causally. The framework represents users as boundedly rational decision makers and encodes their causal beliefs in a graph. The graph therefore concerns the user’s perception of causal relationships, which becomes part of the relevance prediction model.

The authors show how even limited information about this graph can help address changes in the data distribution. The proposed route to robustness is to incorporate information about the process behind users’ judgments, rather than relying entirely on historical predictive relationships. Experiments in multiple settings demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness, supporting causal user modeling as a useful ingredient for relevance prediction under changing content.
neurips-2022-in-the-eye-of-the-beholder-.tldr: Modeling users’ causal beliefs helps relevance predictors cope with changes in the content and data they encounter.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a network’s connections from measurements governed by a conservation law. In its balance equation, a matrix maps node potentials to externally injected flows, and the matrix’s nonzero pattern describes connectivity. The available data consist of potential measurements and statistical information about injections, rather than complete observations of both.

The method assumes Gaussian injections with known covariance and estimates the connectivity matrix using maximum likelihood with an L1 penalty that encourages sparsity. It targets high-dimensional settings where the network can contain far more nodes than there are observed samples. The authors show that the optimization has a convex objective and a unique solution.

Under a mutual incoherence condition, they establish sufficient relationships among sample count, network size, and graph degree for exact connection recovery with high probability. They also bound matrix estimation error under several norms. Experiments on synthetic and real data complement these guarantees, connecting the statistical analysis to practical recovery of networks governed by balance equations.
neurips-2022-learning-the-structure-of-l.tldr: A sparse likelihood estimator recovers conservation-governed network structure with conditional theoretical guarantees and experimental validation.

paragraphs: A strong action-recognition model should learn video features that remain useful across multiple datasets. Training one model to achieve this is challenging because the learning problem spans multiple collections of examples and action classes. The paper introduces MultiTrain, a Transformer-based training approach designed around this shared representation goal.

MultiTrain adds two loss terms with distinct roles. The informative loss encourages the feature embedding to be expressive. The projection loss works separately for each dataset while uncovering relationships among classes across datasets. Together, these objectives aim to make the learned features informative and connect the class information supplied by different training sources.

The authors evaluate the approach on Kinetics-400, Kinetics-700, Moments-in-Time, Activitynet, and Something-something-v2. They report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art performance in their experiments. The findings support using explicit representation objectives to make multi-dataset training effective, with the contribution centered on how a single model learns across datasets rather than merely adopting a Transformer architecture.
neurips-2022-multi-dataset-training-of-t.tldr: MultiTrain combines informative and cross-dataset projection losses to improve a single Transformer’s action-recognition representations.

paragraphs: Designing photonic devices requires electromagnetic field simulations, but numerical solvers can make repeated design and validation expensive. The paper addresses learning across a family of simulation problems. It contrasts this goal with neural approaches that predict the solution of one partial differential equation instance with predefined parameters.

NeurOLight learns a family of frequency-domain Maxwell equations through a neural operator framework. It represents different devices on a common discretized domain, uses a compact wave prior to express parameterized equations, and encodes incoming light through masked source modeling. Cross-shaped network blocks reduce parameter requirements, while augmentation based on superposition improves data efficiency.

The authors report simulation speeds roughly two orders of magnitude faster than numerical solvers. Against prior neural models, they report approximately 54% lower prediction error with approximately 44% fewer parameters. These findings indicate that a shared representation of devices, parameters, and light sources can support fast parametric simulation while improving prediction quality and model compactness in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2022-neurolight-a-physics-agnost.tldr: NeurOLight learns families of photonic simulations and reports much faster execution with lower error and fewer parameters than prior neural models.

paragraphs: This paper studies a two-stage matching problem in which vertices carry weights and the algorithm receives a suggested matching during the first stage. Advice creates an opportunity to improve decisions, but it also raises a question: how much performance should an algorithm guarantee when the recommendation is unreliable?

The authors formalize that tension using robustness and consistency. Robustness measures guaranteed performance relative to the optimal matching chosen with full information. Consistency measures performance when the advice is correct. They characterize the best achievable boundary between these goals, so the benefit of trusting advice can be compared directly with the protection retained against bad advice.

Their algorithm achieves pairs satisfying sqrt(1−R) + sqrt(1−C) = 1 for robustness R between zero and three quarters. They also prove that no algorithm can improve this tradeoff in the studied problem. Matching an achievable guarantee with an impossibility result makes the boundary exact, rather than simply showing that one particular compromise works.
neurips-2022-online-bipartite-matching-w.tldr: The paper gives an algorithm and matching impossibility bound for the exact robustness–consistency tradeoff in two-stage matching with advice.

paragraphs: Dense vision tasks make global self-attention expensive because the model must reason over many image locations. Coarsening attention can overlook local relationships, while restricting it to local neighborhoods can weaken global modeling. Orthogonal Transformer introduces another way to reduce this cost while preserving access to both kinds of information.

The model computes attention in an orthogonal representation with much lower resolution that can be mapped back to the spatial domain. Every orthogonal token can attend to the full set of visual tokens, supporting global dependencies and local correlations. The transformation uses a matrix constructed to be orthogonal and suitable for optimization within a neural network.

The architecture also includes a Positional MLP to represent position at arbitrary input resolutions and strengthen the MLP component. These pieces are organized into a hierarchical backbone. Experiments show strong performance in classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation, supporting the usefulness of changing the space where attention operates for a broad set of vision tasks.
neurips-2022-orthogonal-transformer-an-e.tldr: Orthogonal Transformer computes attention in a lower-resolution reversible representation to combine efficient processing with local and global visual modeling.

paragraphs: Differentially private data generation aims to make data shareable while providing rigorous privacy guarantees. A major challenge is producing synthetic samples that remain useful, particularly for high-dimensional data. The paper attributes part of this difficulty to the complexity of fitting an entire data distribution under private training.

The proposed method changes the target of optimization. It directly learns a small set of representative samples instead of trying to model the complete distribution. The authors argue that this is generally an easier task and better suited to privacy-constrained training. They also use discriminative information from downstream tasks to guide and simplify the learning process.

This makes the usefulness of the generated set central to the method’s design. The representative samples are optimized with information about tasks they are intended to support. The authors report substantial improvements in sample utility over state-of-the-art approaches, presenting private set generation as an alternative route to useful high-dimensional synthetic data.
neurips-2022-private-set-generation-with.tldr: Directly optimizing a small representative private dataset with downstream task information improves synthetic sample utility.

paragraphs: Unitary matrices can help recurrent and very deep networks maintain stability over long chains of computation. Enforcing this structure, however, can require expensive parameterizations or slow training. projUNN addresses the cost by using rank-k updates, or low-rank approximations to updates, while retaining access to full unitary or orthogonal matrices.

The paper introduces Direct and Tangent variants that use low-rank gradient information to update constrained matrices. For matrices of dimension N, their training runtime scales as O(kN²). The rank therefore provides a way to control the update cost without restricting the model to a smaller family of unitary matrices.

Even with rank one, the authors report performance comparable to baseline implementations. In recurrent networks, projUNN closely matches or exceeds the benchmarked results of earlier unitary methods. Preliminary experiments also explore orthogonal convolutional networks. Those models do not outperform the state of the art, although the authors identify improved stability and robustness at large depth as potential benefits.
neurips-2022-projunn-efficient-method-fo.tldr: projUNN uses low-rank updates to train full unitary or orthogonal matrices efficiently while retaining competitive recurrent-network performance.

paragraphs: A backdoored reinforcement-learning policy can behave normally until an adversary modifies its observations with a hidden trigger. The trigger then causes harmful or unexpected actions during deployment. This paper considers an agent that lacks the resources to retrain a good policy and instead needs to make an existing policy safer to use.

The defense assumes a particular subspace structure for triggers. It estimates a safe subspace using interactions with a clean environment, then projects observations into that subspace before the policy acts. The intervention therefore changes the observations supplied to the policy, using clean experience to identify the representation used for sanitization.

Under the stated assumption, the authors prove approximate optimality within epsilon despite triggers when the clean interaction count is O(D/((1−gamma)^4 epsilon²)). Here D is state dimension and gamma is the discount factor. They also report good empirical performance in two Atari environments. The guarantee links protection to a concrete trigger assumption and a sufficient amount of clean interaction.
neurips-2022-provable-defense-against-ba.tldr: Under a subspace trigger assumption, projecting observations into an estimated safe subspace provides a provable defense without retraining the policy.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much graph learning can be accomplished with a standard Transformer. Its method, TokenGT, represents every node and edge as a separate token, adds token embeddings, and processes the resulting collection with a Transformer. The approach places the graph representation in the input rather than introducing graph-specific changes to the Transformer.

With an appropriate choice of token embeddings, the authors prove that this construction is at least as expressive as a second-order invariant graph network built from equivariant linear layers. That comparison establishes substantial representational capacity, exceeding the message-passing graph neural networks described in the abstract. The embedding choice is an explicit condition of the result.

On the large PCQM4Mv2 graph dataset, TokenGT performs significantly better than the evaluated graph neural network baselines and competitively with Transformers using sophisticated graph-specific biases. Together, the theory and experiment support the idea that carefully tokenized graph inputs can make a standard Transformer a capable graph learner.
neurips-2022-pure-transformers-are-power.tldr: TokenGT turns nodes and edges into tokens, giving standard Transformers strong conditional expressivity guarantees and competitive graph-learning results.

paragraphs: Large networks can often be reduced substantially with little accuracy loss, but repeatedly training, pruning, and retraining is expensive. The lottery-ticket idea proposes finding a sparse subnetwork at initialization that can subsequently train to high accuracy. The practical challenge is showing that the selected subnetwork is better than straightforward alternatives.

The paper highlights evidence that earlier initialization-time selection algorithms failed comparisons such as training randomly chosen sparse subnetworks. Gem-Miner addresses this gap by finding subnetworks at initialization that beat the current baselines. The contribution concerns the quality of the selection procedure, since the chosen sparse networks still undergo training.

The authors report that Gem-Miner’s subnetworks train to accuracy competitive with or better than Iterative Magnitude Pruning. They also report speedups of up to 19 times. These findings support the existence of a useful initialization-time search procedure: its selected networks outperform simple comparisons while offering a faster route to competitive sparse models in the reported evaluations.
neurips-2022-rare-gems-finding-lottery-t.tldr: Gem-Miner finds trainable sparse subnetworks at initialization that beat existing baselines and match or improve pruning accuracy up to 19 times faster.

paragraphs: Graph Transformers need ways to represent graph structure, exchange information along edges, and connect distant nodes. This paper organizes those choices into a common recipe. It first clarifies positional and structural encodings by classifying them as local, global, or relative, helping distinguish the information different designs provide.

The proposed architecture separates aggregation along actual graph edges from global Transformer processing. Its three ingredients are a positional or structural encoding, a local message-passing mechanism, and a global attention mechanism. The authors present an architecture with complexity linear in the numbers of nodes and edges and argue that this separation preserves expressivity through universal function approximation on graphs.

GraphGPS implements the recipe as a modular framework supporting multiple encoding and processing choices. Evaluation on 16 benchmarks produces highly competitive results across all of them. The findings support combining local and global mechanisms while keeping their design choices modular, making it possible to pursue scalability and representational strength within the same framework.
neurips-2022-recipe-for-a-general-powerf.tldr: GraphGPS combines structural encodings, local message passing, and global attention in a modular graph Transformer recipe with linear-complexity architecture.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning for a controlled queue whose jobs may leave when kept waiting. The objective balances energy consumption with user-perceived performance. Although the system has a birth-and-death structure, its Markov decision process can have an enormous diameter, making general regret bounds suggest that learning could be inefficient.

The authors analyze a slightly modified UCRL2 algorithm using the queue’s particular structure. Their regret bound scales, up to logarithmic factors, as the square root of E2 times the number of actions and elapsed time. E2 is a weighted second moment of the stationary distribution under a reference policy, and it is bounded independently of the number of states.

The resulting bound is asymptotically independent of both state count and diameter. A central part of the proof tracks how unevenly the learner visits different states. This shows why treating every state through general size and diameter measures can be overly pessimistic for this structured queueing problem.
neurips-2022-reinforcement-learning-in-a.tldr: Exploiting a queue’s birth-and-death structure yields a regret bound asymptotically independent of its state count and enormous diameter.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search automates the choice of network structure. This paper argues that the search should account for differences in the importance of input elements, such as image pixels. If some parts of an input matter more for a prediction, that information can also guide how candidate architectures are trained and evaluated.

The proposed framework joins four learning stages. First, it trains a model while temporarily fixing its architecture. Second, it generates saliency maps from that model. Third, it retrains using inputs reweighted by those maps. Fourth, it evaluates validation loss and updates the architecture to improve that loss.

These stages form a unified four-level optimization problem, allowing the saliency information to change during the search. Architecture selection is therefore linked to what the current model considers informative in the data. Experiments on several datasets demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness, supporting the use of dynamic input importance as part of automated architecture design.
neurips-2022-saliency-aware-neural-archi.tldr: A four-stage optimization framework uses dynamically estimated input saliency to guide neural architecture search.

paragraphs: The paper considers minimax optimization where one set of variables minimizes an objective and another maximizes it. The objective is smooth, strongly convex in the minimizing variables, and strongly concave in the maximizing variables. For this problem class, a known lower bound specifies how many gradient evaluations may be required to reach a desired accuracy.

Earlier algorithms exceeded that lower bound by extra logarithmic factors. The proposed method removes this gap, requiring O(sqrt(kappa_x kappa_y) log(1/epsilon)) gradient evaluations. The two condition numbers describe the conditioning associated with strong convexity and strong concavity, while epsilon specifies the target accuracy.

The construction has three parts: reformulate the minimax problem as minimization using a pointwise conjugate, apply a particular proximal point method, and approximately compute its proximal steps with an optimal monotone-inclusion procedure. Matching the lower bound establishes optimal gradient-evaluation complexity for the stated problem class, giving a precise sense in which the algorithm is optimal.
neurips-2022-the-first-optimal-algorithm.tldr: A reformulation and carefully computed proximal steps achieve the known optimal gradient-evaluation complexity for smooth strongly convex–strongly concave minimax problems.

paragraphs: The paper revisits how Mixup enters a classifier’s training objective. Its proposed change, RegMixup, retains standard cross-entropy training and adds Mixup as a regularizer. This changes the balance of training signals while preserving Mixup’s role in influencing the learned model.

The motivation includes a problem with uncertainty estimation. The authors observe that ordinary Mixup can perform poorly at detecting examples from outside the training distribution. Their empirical analysis suggests a possible explanation: models may produce high-entropy predictions broadly, making familiar and unfamiliar examples difficult to distinguish through predictive uncertainty.

Experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-10/100 compare RegMixup with recent uncertainty-estimation approaches. The authors report improved accuracy and, in most evaluated cases, significantly better uncertainty estimates under covariate shifts and out-of-distribution detection. The findings show that the way Mixup is combined with the ordinary classification objective can affect both prediction quality and the usefulness of uncertainty, while the high-entropy explanation remains an empirically supported possibility.
neurips-2022-using-mixup-as-a-regularize.tldr: RegMixup adds Mixup to standard cross-entropy as a regularizer, improving accuracy and uncertainty estimation in most evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference often requires working with a posterior distribution that is difficult to summarize directly. Variational inference addresses this by constructing a simpler approximation whose summary statistics are easier to compute. The paper focuses on strengthening the algorithmic foundations of this approach, which are less developed than those of Markov chain Monte Carlo.

The proposed methods approximate the posterior with a Gaussian distribution or a mixture of Gaussians. Their design draws on gradient flows in Bures–Wasserstein space, a geometric setting for Gaussian probability distributions. This treats improvement of the approximation as motion through a space of distributions rather than only as an unconstrained choice of numerical parameters.

When the target posterior is log-concave, the methods come with strong theoretical guarantees. That condition defines the stated setting for the guarantees. The contribution connects practical families of approximating distributions with a principled optimization framework, providing a route to analyzing variational inference with theoretical assurance comparable in spirit to established sampling methodology.
neurips-2022-variational-inference-via-w.tldr: Wasserstein gradient flows provide principled Gaussian and Gaussian-mixture variational inference methods with strong guarantees for log-concave targets.
